hints: The period describes a time interval, not a distance between wavefronts.
Think of watching one point in the medium complete a full repeated motion.
State the interval for one full oscillation or wave cycle; an equivalent wavefront-at-a-point description is also valid.
walkthrough: At a fixed point, the wave motion repeats after one complete cycle.
The period is the time taken for that one complete oscillation or cycle.
For a progressive wave, it can also be described as the time between successive wavefronts passing the same point.

ai_rubric.observable: States that period is the time for one complete oscillation or wave cycle, or an equivalent interval between successive wavefronts passing the same point.

hints: Think about what happens at a point where more than one wave is present.
The principle needs both the overlap condition and the rule for combining displacements.
State what the resultant displacement equals when waves meet.
walkthrough: Superposition applies where two or more waves overlap at a point.
At that point, their individual displacements combine algebraically.
Therefore the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the principle applies when two or more waves meet or overlap at a point.
States that the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.

hints: Use the stated wavelength of 0.040 m to locate the wave in the electromagnetic spectrum.
Compare 4 cm with the broad wavelength ranges for radio, microwave, infrared and visible radiation.
Select the spectrum region that includes centimetre-scale wavelengths.
walkthrough: The wavelength is 0.040 m, which is 4 cm.
Centimetre-scale electromagnetic wavelengths lie in the microwave region of the spectrum.
The waves from X and Y are microwaves.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the 0.040 m electromagnetic waves as microwaves.

hints: Electromagnetic waves travel at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum.
Combine wave speed with the definition of period to express the speed as wavelength divided by period.
Calculate T in seconds from T = λ / c, then convert seconds to picoseconds using 1 ps = 10⁻¹² s.
walkthrough: For a wave, v = fλ and f = 1/T, so v = λ/T.
Rearrange for the period: T = λ/v = 0.040 / (3.00 × 10⁸).
To two significant figures, the period is 130 ps.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses v = λ/T, or equivalently v = fλ together with f = 1/T.
Substitutes the 0.040 m wavelength and 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ vacuum speed to calculate the period in seconds.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: The calculation finds a path-length difference and expresses it in wavelengths using division; it uses no major reusable syllabus physics formula.

hints: Path difference is the difference between the distances travelled from X and Y to the same point Z.
First subtract the two stated source-to-detector distances in metres.
Divide that path difference by the 0.040 m wavelength to express it as a number of wavelengths.
walkthrough: The two path lengths to Z are 1.380 m and 1.240 m.
The path difference is 1.380 − 1.240 = 0.140 m.
Express it in wavelengths: 0.140 / 0.040 = 3.5.
The path difference at Z is 3.5λ.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates (1.380 − 1.240) / 0.040 and shows that the path difference is 3.5 wavelengths.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: The calculation converts a path difference expressed in wavelengths into cycles and phase angle; it uses no major reusable syllabus physics formula.

hints: One whole wavelength corresponds to one complete cycle of phase change.
Use the 3.5-wavelength path difference established in part (c)(iii).
Multiply the number of wavelengths by 360°; the resulting angle may also be written as its equivalent within one cycle.
walkthrough: A path difference of one wavelength corresponds to a phase difference of 360°.
At Z, the path difference is 3.5λ.
The phase difference is 3.5 × 360° = 1260°.
Subtracting complete 360° cycles gives the equivalent phase difference 180°.

ai_rubric.observable: Converts the 3.5-wavelength path difference to 1260°, or gives the equivalent phase difference of 180°.

hints: Use the phase difference at Z from the preceding part to decide how the two waves combine.
Equal-amplitude waves that arrive in antiphase cancel their displacements at the detector.
Relate zero resultant amplitude to the intensity at Z.
walkthrough: The 180° phase difference means that the two waves arrive in antiphase at Z.
Their amplitudes are equal, so their displacements cancel completely by destructive interference.
The resultant amplitude is zero, and intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
The intensity at Z is zero.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the intensity at Z is zero.

hints: In a vacuum, electromagnetic waves keep the same wave speed when their frequency changes.
Use the wave-speed relationship to decide how a lower frequency changes the wavelength.
Interference maxima and minima require particular path differences measured in wavelengths; relate a longer wavelength to their spacing along the detector path.
walkthrough: The waves still travel at the speed of light in vacuum, so c = fλ.
When frequency decreases while c stays constant, wavelength increases.
The path-difference change required to move between successive interference maxima or minima is therefore larger.
Adjacent intensity maxima and adjacent minima are farther apart along the detector path.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the distance between adjacent intensity maxima or adjacent minima increases.
